readnow.text: No new chapter today. Keep Chapters 10 to 12 open in your book as you choose your theme.

warmup.text: Today you name the theme. First, read the eagle poem again. You found two themes in six lines. Now look for two themes in one scene from the novel.

words.text: Explain the roots and the endings in your own words. Pick an option on the choice board. The last six pans fill Jack's pouch.

reading.text: Choose a theme claim, or write your own. Find a second piece of evidence. Then argue the other side yourself, and answer it with evidence from the book.

assignment.text: Read your literary response once more. Check the claim, the two choices, the transitions, and the closing. Then submit it, and copy your work into Canvas.

do: Tap the highlighted word in the first sentence.
Write the second sentence correctly in your reading journal.
Tap See the Answer to check.
how.why: Transitions and openers tell a reader how one idea connects to the next.

do: Read the poem out loud twice.
Read the tip.
Answer the question in your reading journal.
how.why: A short poem can carry two themes at once. Spotting both trains you to find more than one theme in the novel.

do: Read the question.
Write 2 or 3 sentences in your reading journal.
Then go on to Word Study.
how.why: Thinking before you read gives you something to watch for.

do: Explain the two roots in your reading journal.
Type the word that fits each sentence.
Tap Check My Work.
how.why: Explaining a root shows you really know it.

do: Read the four options.
Pick one and say which at the top of the box.
Use all five words.
how.why: This is your Show What You Know for vocabulary this week.

do: Read the before and after.
Tap the right answer in each question.
Answer the question in your reading journal.
how.why: Explaining a choice shows you can make it on purpose.

do: Answer the question in your reading journal.
Tap the right spelling in each pair.
how.why: Knowing how the base changes keeps the ending right.

do: Read the three lenses.
Tap the one you will use today.
Keep it in mind as you read. You will use it at the end.
how.why: Naming the theme pulls the whole week together.
how.use: You will use it in theme question 1.

do: Read the four theme claims.
Pick one, or write your own.
Answer the three theme questions.
how.why: A theme claim is only as strong as its evidence.

do: Pick a theme you did not choose.
Write the best case for it in 1 or 2 sentences.
Answer it with your own evidence.
how.why: Answering the other side makes your own claim stronger.

do: Read your response once more.
Put the whole response in the box.
Copy your work and paste it into Canvas.
how.why: A literary response proves a theme with what characters choose to do.

game.title: Pan for Color
game.sub: This week's word game · 6 pans today
game.look: Each pan holds four words from the diggings. Two are color, the real gold. Two are slickens, the mud. Tap the slickens to wash them over the side. When only gold is left, the spangles slide into Jack's pouch.

do: Read the clue on the pan.
Tap a word that does not belong to wash it out.
Keep going until only gold is left.
Tap Next pan.
how.why: A real ending is spelled the same way every time, and a real root carries its meaning into every word it builds.

game.doneLine: Four days, twenty-four pans. Jack's pouch is full of color.

pans.clue: Wash out the misspelled words. Keep the gold.

chips.why: careless + ness: two s's and then two more.
careless + ness keeps every s: carelessness.
-ness has two s's: dampness.
damp + ness.

pans.clue: Wash out the misspelled words. Keep the gold.

chips.why: settle keeps its e before -ment: settlement.
settle keeps its e before -ment.
agree + ment.
The ending is -ment: agreement.

pans.clue: Wash out the misspelled words. Keep the gold.

chips.why: probable becomes probabil before -ity.
Do not drop the i before -ty: probability.
The ending is -ity: prosperity.
prosper + ity.

pans.clue: Wash out the words with no real fort or val root. Keep the gold.

chips.why: dis + com + fort (strong): a feeling of not being at ease.
arrival comes from a word for reaching the shore. No val root.
festival comes from a word for a feast. No val root.
val (worth) + uation: a judgment of what something is worth.

pans.clue: Wash out the words with no real fort or val root. Keep the gold.

chips.why: fortunately comes from fortune, a word for luck. No fort (strong) root.
un + com + fort (strong) + ably: not at ease.
under + val (worth) + ue: to think something is worth less than it is.
interval comes from a word for the space between walls. No val root.

pans.clue: Wash out the words with no real fort or val root. Keep the gold.

chips.why: fort (strong) + ifications: walls that make a place strong.
forty is a number word. No fort root.
e + val (worth) + uating: judging what something is worth.
rival comes from a word for a stream. No val root.

virtue.name: honesty
virtue.title: The most honest moment this week
virtue.intro: Look back at Chapters 10 to 12. Tap the moment you think shows honesty the most.

options.t: On the stage, Praiseworthy tells the road agent he is not a gentleman, merely a butler (Chapter 10).
Praiseworthy writes to warn Dr. Buckbee about Cut-Eye Higgins and the map (Chapter 11).
Back in Hangtown, Praiseworthy tries to tell the miners the story has been exaggerated (Chapter 12).

art.title: Among the Sierra Nevada, California
art.alt: A large painting of a calm mountain lake with deer at the water's edge, tall cliffs and a waterfall on the left, and snowy peaks lit by sunlight breaking through clouds.
art.look: Albert Bierstadt painted this in 1868, after travels in the mountains where the gold camps were. He made the light and the peaks grander than real life. Look at the storm clouds and the sunlight breaking through at the same time. One painting, two feelings, like a poem or a novel that carries two themes.
